nodes.title: Tense agreement
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: Verbs must agree with their subject in person and number, and tense must match the time of the action. Words like 'yesterday', 'last week' and 'ago' signal the past tense; 'tomorrow', 'next week' and 'soon' signal the future. When rewriting a sentence into a different tense, change the main verb but keep the meaning the same: 'She writes a letter' (present) → 'She wrote a letter' (past).

nodes.title: Articles: a, an, the
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: Use 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound. The rule is about the sound, not the spelling: it is 'an honest girl' because 'honest' begins with a vowel sound, but 'a university' because 'university' begins with a 'y' (consonant) sound. Use 'the' when the listener already knows which specific thing is meant.

nodes.title: Finding the main idea
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: The main idea of a passage is the single point the writer wants you to take away. Look for a sentence that summarises the whole passage rather than naming one supporting detail. When a question asks for the main idea, do not pick the most interesting detail or the first sentence by default — pick the statement that covers every other sentence in the passage.

nodes.title: Vocabulary in context
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: Many words have more than one meaning. To work out which meaning is used, read the whole sentence and look for clues — the surrounding nouns, the verb the word qualifies, and whether the tone is positive or negative. 'Ripe' means 'ready to eat' when used with a fruit, but 'ready to happen' when used with 'the time was ripe'.

nodes.title: Basic punctuation
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: End every statement with a full stop, every question with a question mark, and every exclamation with an exclamation mark. Capitalise the first word of a sentence, proper nouns (names of people, places, months, days), and the pronoun 'I'. Use commas to separate items in a list and to separate a dependent clause that comes before the main clause.

nodes.title: Commonly misspelled words
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: Many spelling mistakes come from writing what a word sounds like rather than how it is actually spelled. 'Receive' follows the 'i before e except after c' pattern. 'Separate' has an 'a' in the middle (think 'a rat in separate'). 'Government' contains the word 'govern' plus '-ment'. Proofread by reading your work aloud — your ear will catch slips your eye misses.

nodes.title: Figures of speech
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as' ('as brave as a lion'). A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as' ('Time is money'). Personification gives human qualities to non-human things ('The wind whispered'). Hyperbole is exaggeration for effect ('a million times'). Irony is a contrast between what is said and what is meant, or between expectation and reality.

nodes.title: Summary and paraphrase
nodes.subject: english
nodes.body_markdown: A summary keeps the main idea but cuts the supporting detail. A paraphrase keeps all the meaning but changes the wording. To paraphrase, replace key words with synonyms and rearrange the sentence structure — but do not change the meaning. A good summary or paraphrase passes the test: someone who has not read the original can understand the same idea from your version.
